Dear Reviewer qGKy,

Thank you for your quick response. If we understand your comment correctly, you are questioning why simulated spectra are useful for machine learning given that there is inevitably going to be a (bigger or smaller) distribution shift between the experimental and simulated spectra. Please correct us if this is incorrect. 

We can completely understand your concern and only committed the resources to generating this dataset based on prior success in using simulated data to pretrain models for structure elucidation. The main reason for using simulated data lies in the availability of experimental data. For example, for IR spectroscopy there are only around 20k publicly available spectra. While this is better than nothing it is hard to train models for structure elucidation solely on these spectra. As such we turned to simulating spectra, pretraining the model on those spectra followed by finetuning on experimental spectra. We most extensively studied this on IR spectroscopy (currently under review). The following table outlines four cases: First we evaluate a model pretrained on simulated data zero shot on the NIST IR database. As expected, the performance is not great due to the relatively large distribution shift between simulated and experimental IR spectra. Next, we train a model from scratch on the NIST database, again the performance is not great as it was only trained on ~5k spectra. The next experiment is the outlined pretraining and finetuning. This model performs significantly better than either of the two previous ones. One may argue at this point that the model only learned how to generate molecules but did not gain any benefit from the IR spectrum. To demonstrate that this is not the case we finetune the pretrained model on mirrored experimental spectra. Mirrored in this case means that the orientation of the spectrum is reversed from pretraining to finetuning, i.e. the peaks are in different positions. Here, we again observe a notably smaller performance showing that the model is able to derive information from the IR spectrum during pretraining.

|-|-|-|-
Zero Shot | 1.09 | 2.89 | 3.48
Train from Scratch on NIST | 14.74 | 36.99 | 40.75
Pretrained + Finetuned on NIST | 44.39 | 66.85 | 69.79
Pretrained + Finetuned on NIST (mirrored) | 21.98 | 46.34 | 52.32

Another piece of evidence is the zero-shot performance of the models on the van Bramer and Basten dataset in the structure elucidation task. The performance is shown in the table below and demonstrates that even if the models were trained on simulated the zero shot performance can still be relatively high. At this point, we would like to thank you again for pointing out the shortcomings of CFM-ID. Dear Reviewer vx3L,

First of all we would like to thank you for taking the time to read and evaluate our manuscript. Below we have addressed each of your concerns chronologically.

__Hard to establish the link from single-modal molecule prediction (tasks defined in this benchmark) to structure elucidation__

We appreciate your review of our paper and would like to clarify our approach. Our aim was to demonstrate the versatility of this dataset across multiple tasks, such as predicting spectra from molecular structures and vice versa. Our findings indicate that currently, no single modality is sufficient for our baseline architectures to determine molecular structure reliably from a single spectrum type. We anticipate that our dataset will facilitate the development of more sophisticated multi-modal architectures capable of performing structure elucidation with higher accuracy using various spectral inputs.

__Alternative methods of representation__

We frequently employ vector representations for spectra, as this approach aligns well with their inherent nature. However, we also explored various alternative representations. For instance, we represented $^1$H-NMR spectra as lists of peaks (text) rather than continuous vectors. For molecules, we utilized SMILES notation which is a text representation. There is certainly potential for future work to explore different molecular representations (e.g. generating a graph instead of SMILES). Inspired by your comment, we have added a sentence addressing this possibility in our "Other tasks to explore" section. *___Representations:___ While our study utilized SMILES as the primary form to represent molecules there are a variety of different chemical representations that could be explored, reaching from SELFIES[1], deep-SMILES[2] as well as generating graph instead of a text-based representation.  Additionally, the spectral information could be represented in various ways. For instance, generating figures from vector representations and employing image-based models*.

__Choosing “molecules with more than five and fewer than 35 heavy atoms”__

In our initial research, we employed a comparable molecular preprocessing pipeline for compounds sourced from PubChem. During this process, we observed that larger PubChem molecules typically consist of complex structures, such as extensive metal-organic frameworks. These molecules are generally unsuitable for the simulation methods we intend to apply. Hence, the criterion was still there to have a fair evaluation between models trained on the two datasets, which is not the scope of this work.

__Nested Rings__

We agree that nested rings present an interesting case to demonstrate the capabilities of the model due to the increased complexity of the molecules. As such we have analysed the top-1, top-5, and top-10 accuracy in predicting the correct structure for these molecules. A table is shown below. Although we observe a slight decline in performance compared to simpler structures, the drop is generally modest, underscoring the model's robustness in handling more intricate molecular configurations. In addition, we have attached a pdf file with some examples of molecules containing nested rings.

| MS/MS (Positive, CFM-ID)   |17.43        |    32.4   |    37.24   |       20.98       |   39.32   |    44.93   |
| MS/MS (Negative, CFM-ID)   |         14.85        |   29.14   |    32.39   |       23.53       |   42.59   |    47.53   |

__Information that one spectrum type cannot provide, which could be complemented by another, should be explored.__

We investigated this phenomenon using NMR spectra, as they allow us to observe the influence of each modality on overall performance. We created three datasets, each consisting of molecules containing one of the following functional groups: chlorine, iodine, or alkyne. For each dataset, we examined the top-1 accuracy in spectra elucidation for the $^{1}$H-NMR alone, $^{13}$C-NMR alone and $^{13}$C & $^{1}$H-NMR together.
For the chlorine and iodine datasets, we observed that the top-1 accuracy of models trained on single modalities increased when modalities were combined. The alkyne dataset presented the most interesting case. There, the performance of single-modal models was 52% for $^{1}$H-NMR and 54% for $^{13}$C-NMR. However, when trained on both modalities together, the accuracy increased to 66%.


__A more detailed discussion of combining multiple spectra in the future work section__

Thank you for the suggestion. We have added the following paragraph to the future work section:
*Multimodal Approaches: Combining the different types of spectra for a true multimodal model presents is significantly harder than e.g. predicting the structure from a single modality. Not only does the best representation for each modality need to be considered but also how to combine the different modalities. We suggest the following approach: First optimise the representation for each modality individually before considering how to combine them. Here the approaches range from early fusion, in practice often a simple concatenation of the different modalities, over medium fusion, embed each modality then fuse, to late fusion. Another consideration is how to process each modality and weight each modality. Each of these factors would need to be considered when building a multimodal model.*

__Quality of the data is as good as the method employed for calculating the spectra, ML model built on the dataset should be considered with caution.__

We are aware of this limitation, thanks for helping us improve our manuscript by making this point more clear, we opted to expand the limitation section: *However, the dataset also has multiple limitations, the largest being that all data is simulated. As a result, there is a distribution shift between simulated and experimental spectra and models trained on the data in this set will likely benefit from further finetuning on experimental spectra. The efficacy of these models is inherently determined by the fidelity of the underlying simulation used to generate the spectra.*

In addition, we have conducted a further assessment of the similarity between the simulated and experimental spectra. Please see the general comment for more detail. 

__Experimental validation with a larger number of molecules will make it more comprehensive.__

Thank you for pointing out this issue. We have validated the similarity between the simulated and experimental spectra on larger datasets. Please refer to the general comment.

__A proper list of hyperparameters tuned for model building is not provided__

Our aim with the benchmarks was to use models off the shelf models with as little modification as possible. All transformer models were trained using the OpenNMT library with the hyperparameters adapted from the Molecular Transformer[1]. In previous papers we conducted hyperparameter tuning for models trained on NMR and IR spectra. However, this did not result in any performance gains and as such we did not modify the hyperparameters further for this project. The CNN model we use was specifically built for functional group classification from IR spectra by Jung et. al. In their paper, an extensive hyperparameter screen is conducted.
As mentioned in the top comment we have performed five fold cross validation to improve the reliability of our results. In contrast to the experiments conducted in the original manuscript these were run with an 80/20/5 train, test and validation split.

__Missing checklist point number 2 and 5.__

Thanks for spotting this mistake, we added and answered the requested checklist section. Both are not applicable to this work and we have updated the checklist.

__License not added in the GitHub repository.__

The License was added to the GitHub Repository.

__Total amount of compute time not given for XGBoost and 1DCNN models.__

We train the XGBoost classifiers on 32 CPU cores. Below are the run times for each modality:

- MSMS: 58 minutes

An analysis, of each simulation method can be found in the pdf attached to this comment.

Dear Reviewers,

We would like to thank all reviewers for providing constructive feedback that helped us improved the paper. We are encouraged that reviews think our dataset is:

- "the field will benefit from a common resource for simulated data. I would use this dataset in my own research." (Reviewer x5D8)
- "the paper proposed an important benchmark the authors has made great effort to make this data accessible to the community. (Reviewer vx3L)
- "A very large dataset and multimodal spectra is the major strength of the paper." (Reviewer yKuK)
- "This paper tackles a really important problem and the workflow is realistic" (Reviewer qGKy)

We have been working hard to improve the paper on several fronts, addressing your critique. Below, we summarise the major changes that we have made in an updated draft. In addition, we respond to each reviewer individually. 

**Suitability of CFM-ID:** 

We would like to thank reviewer x5D8 and qGKy in raising the limitations of CFM-ID and the related literature. We opted to simulate the MS-MS spectrum of all molecules in the dataset using the two best-performing models mentioned by the reviewers (Iceberg and Scarf) for two ionization modes ([M+] and [M+H]). Rather than replacing spectra simulated with CFM-ID, we add the new spectra to the dataset, so other researchers have a large set of mechanistically simulated spectra to compare to as well. The new data can be found in the updated Zenodo repository. The methodology section of the manuscript, the baseline models as well as the relevance work section of the paper will be updated to reflect the additional simulations. We also provide an analysis of the similarity to experimental spectra of the newly simulated MSMS spectra. 

**Real to Sim Gap:** 

We thank reviewer x5D8, yKuK and qGKy for suggesting improvements in the way we assess the similarity between the simulated and experimental spectra. In addition, to comparing the similarity of the simulated spectra we have compared it to several larger databases of experimental spectra. The suggestion of reviewer x5D8 to use the similarity of the simulated spectrum to the experimental spectrum of the molecule with the closest Tanimoto match was particularly interesting. We are pleased to report that all simulation methods are able to pass this hurdle. |$^{1}$H-NMR + $^{13}$C-NMR|50.31|63.98|67.08

__USPTO selects for synthesizability__

We will be adding the following to paragraph 2 of section 5 (Conclusions and Limitations): *Another limitation is the chemical space covered by USPTO. The USPTO dataset contains molecules sourced from patents and as a result is biased towards synthesisable molecules with applications in industry. On the other hand this means that models trained on our dataset may not perform as well on e.g. natural products.*

__Suitability of CFM-ID__

Thanks for this suggestion, based on the mentioned paper we opted to simulate the MSMS spectrum for all molecules with Iceberg and Scarf. Please see the general comment for more detail.

__Missing error bars__

We have added error bars to all tables. Please see the general comment for more details.

__"Since most spectral data is acquired after a reaction has been completed" -- this is not true of e.g. omics biology, natural products.__

Thanks for spotting this inaccuracy. We have changed the sentence to: *Since in organic chemistry spectral data is often acquired during reactions to monitor progress or after completion, ...*

__Compare the experimental spectrum to the experimental spectrum of a nearest-neighbor in structural space__

Thank you for this suggestion. We have added this evaluation to the similarity segment (see the general comment). As can be seen all, simulation methods clear this hurdle.

__CosineGreedy similarity, which is used on one of the NMR modalities (why not both?)__

The reason lies in the difference between $^1$H- and $^{13}$C-NMR spectra. Where for $^{13}$C-NMR spectra only the position and to a very much lesser extent the integration of the peaks contain information, the shape of the peak e.g. doublet, triplet, etc. contains a wealth of information in $^1$H-NMR spectra. In this regard $^1$H-NMR are more similar to IR spectra where the shape and profile of the peak matter compared to the stick spectra of both MSMS and  $^{13}$C-NMR. As such we utilise the cosine similarity to compare between the vector form of the $^1$H-NMR-spectra.

__What is "accuracy" here? Exact character match of predicted vs true SMILES?__

Thank you for this question, to clarify accuracy is defined as the exact character match of the predicted vs the true SMILES string. All SMILES in the dataset are canonicalized and in addition, we canonicalize all predicted SMILES strings after generation. We added also a full definition of the metric used in the appendix.

__Computational resources used to generate the data__

Thank you for pointing this out. We have listed the compute resources used in the paper below and will be adding them to the Appendix:
- IR: 500 CPU cores with 1TB RAM for ca. 46 days.
- $^1$H-NMR: 200 CPU cores with 400GB RAM for ca. 15 days.
- $^{13}$C-NMR: 200 CPU cores with 400GB RAM for ca. 14 days.
- MSMS-CFM ID: 80 CPU cores with 160GB RAM for ca. 7 days.
- MSMS-Iceberg: 16 CPU cores with 32GB RAM for ca. 3 days.
- MSMS-Scarf:  16 CPU with 32GB RAM cores for ca. 1.5 days
All simulations were run on AMD EPYC 7452 CPUs.

__Commentary on the state of currently available MS/MS datasets__

Thanks for this suggestion, we added the following statement: *As with NMR and IR spectra, the datasets used for training mass spectrometry models are often not publicly accessible. These datasets typically require a commercial license for access, such as the NIST MS database. However, efforts to create open-access repositories of experimentally measured data are underway, with the GNPS database[1] being a notable example.*

A very useful contribution for pretraining models. As real datasets remain small, simulation is an essential tool in developing deep-learning methods for structural elucidation, and the field will benefit from a common resource for simulated data. I would use this dataset in my own research.

Well written with good figures.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: A more thorough investigation of the real-simulated gap would be valuable. In particular, in addition to the train-test split of the simulation spectra, it would help to see numbers for the benchmark evaluations using the experimental spectra from Van Bramer and Bastin as the test set. (If this is already what is happening, it should be clarified.)

limitations.value:
Using USPTO structures selects for synthesizability, so models trained on this dataset may not generalize beyond it, e.g. to natural product space. This is acceptable as long as it is pointed out.

I am not closely familiar with NMR or IR, but the simulation gap for MS/MS is large, and recent ML efforts (e.g. https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/acs.analchem.3c04654) considerably outperform CFM-ID.

correctness.value:
Tables 2-5: missing error bars.

3: "Since most spectral data is acquired after a reaction has been completed" -- this is not true of e.g. omics biology, natural products.

"For example, in the case of NMR spectra, even if the shape and integral are accurately simulated, a slight peak shift compared to the experimentally measured spectrum (a common effect caused by the solvent [58]) can result in a drastic reduction in cosine similarity." -- the CosineGreedy similarity, which is used on one of the NMR modalities (why not both?), is intended to account for this.

summary_and_contributions.value:
The paper presents a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate machine learning models (e.g., transformers) on practical chemistry task (e.g., structure elucidation - deducing molecule structure from the given spectrum). The key contributions of this work include:
•	A large-scale spectroscopic dataset (790k molecules extracted from patent) that covers NMR, MASS, IR spectrums, which are practically used in real-world chemistry situation.
•	Formation of five representative chemistry tasks, such as IR Spectrum prediction, MASS spectrum prediction, etc.
•	Systematic evaluation for structure elucidation, functional group evaluation and spectrum prediction (reverse for structure elucidation)

review.value:
Pros:
•	The paper introduced an interesting research problem for AI community, that is to deduce molecules from the spectroscopic data.
•	The dataset collected is comprehensive and of large-scale.
•	The benchmarks and findings will catalyze more research on AI models for chemistry.
Cons:
•	As authors claims in the introduction, structure elucidation is a complex process. It involves combination of information from different spectrums to deduce accurate molecule structures. It is hard to establish the link from single-modal molecule prediction (tasks defined in this benchmark) to structure elucidation.
•	There is a lack of discussion about the performance of current models. For instance, Table 3 shows that the top accuracy across all tasks is around 10%, but the paper does not explore the reasons behind these low scores.
•	The paper does not discuss alternative methods of representation. Besides vector representation, it does not consider or suggest other potential approaches.

strengths.value: The paper proposed an important benchmark in solving molecule structures from the spectrum data and the authors has made great effort to make this data accessible to the community, e.g., the GitHub documentation is well-organized.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
•	In section 3, what is the reason to choose “molecules with more than five and fewer than 35 heavy atoms”? The paper could benefit from a more thorough discussion of the difficulty of solving these selected molecules with MASS spectrum. Also, I am curious how the model would behave when facing with complicated molecules (e.g. molecules with nested rings).
•	The work benchmarks the process of solving molecular structures using each type of spectrum individually. It would be beneficial to discuss the limitations of each type of spectral data. For instance, the unique information that one spectrum type cannot provide, which could be complemented by another, should be explored.
•	Since structure elucidation is complex, as it takes all kinds of spectrums into account, the paper could benefit from a more detailed discussion of combining them in the future work section.

correctness.value: Overall, I did not find any obvious issues with the correctness of claims.

summary_and_contributions.value: The authors are providing a big (790k) multimodal spectral dataset of small molecules from the USPTO dataset and it is proposed to be useful in expediting automated synthesis.

strengths.value: A very large dataset and multimodal spectra is the major strength of the paper.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
Since the quality of the data is as good as the method employed for calculating the spectra, ML model built on the dataset should be considered with caution. Experimental validation with a larger number of molecules will make it more comprehensive. (See limitations)
For the ML model results (Table 3 and Table 4), error bars or standard deviation (sd) over multiple model runs are not reported. However, in the checklist, it is marked as N/A and thus should be added.
Although the model hyperparameters are given, a proper list of hyperparameters tuned for model building is not provided. The data split shows only a 90:10 train and test ratio. What was the validation split and how were the hyperparameters tuned?
The authors have not responded to the checklist point number 2 (“if you are including theoretical results..” and 5 (“If you used crowdsourcing…”)
Minor: (a) License not added in the GitHub repository. (b) Total amount of compute time not given for XGBoost and 1DCNN models. (c) Citation missing for the boosted tree classifier in the 6th line of the “Functional Group Prediction” section.

limitations.value:
The major limitation, as the author mentioned, is that all the spectral data are simulated. In the ‘Experimental versus Simulated Spectra’ section, the authors have compared the spectra of 251 molecules, covering only 0.0317% of the total 790k molecules. While the intention was to simulate the spectra of realistic molecules from USPTO, the main objective was to generate high-quality spectra. A higher fraction, at least a few thousand molecules outside USPTO and experimentally known spectra (wherever possible), should be compared. For instance, as the authors mentioned, the NIST Gas-Phase IR database contains around ~5k spectra. Thus, a more robust evaluation of the statistical validity of the comparison would enhance the work.
Failure modes of experimental vs. simulated spectra should be provided. An analysis of functional groups or compound types where the simulated spectra differ significantly compared to the experiment would guide users.

title.value: A new dataset integrating experimental characterizations for molecular structures

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper proposes a new dataset comprising three crucial experimental characterization techniques for molecular structures, mass spectrometry, nuclear magnetic resonance, and infrared spectroscopy. The dataset is constructed by processing the reaction database, USPTO. The proposed two tasks are commonly used and realistic, structure elucidation and spectra prediction (from structure to measurement and from measurement to structure). In general, I think this paper tackles a very important challenge in the field, but I have serious concerns about the simulated data (especially mass spectra where the selected approach, CFM-ID 4.0 is no longer a competitive approach in its related literature), also there exists public database to filter from.

review.value:
Out of the three methods, I am only confident in speaking/evaluating mass spectra. My main concern is about dataset construction. CFM-ID is no longer a competitive approach anymore [1, 2, 3, 4]. 

Also another choice is to use experiment dataset, even though NIST is not available, GNPS database has also been filtered (see Repo: https://github.com/samgoldman97/ms-pred) as a publicly available data source for related works.

Regarding evaluation metrics and dataset split, binned cosine similarity and mass spectrum cosine similarity (using hungarian algorithm), and random split/scaffold split are commonly used. You can check relevant references for details [1, 2, 3], for hungarian cosine similarity, check [3, 4].

[1] Goldman, S., Li, J. and Coley, C.W., 2024. Generating molecular fragmentation graphs with autoregressive neural networks. Analytical Chemistry.

[2] Goldman, S., Bradshaw, J., Xin, J. and Coley, C., 2023. Prefix-tree decoding for predicting mass spectra from molecules. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 36, pp.48548-48572.

[3] Murphy, M., Jegelka, S., Fraenkel, E., Kind, T., Healey, D. and Butler, T., 2023, July. Efficiently predicting high resolution mass spectra with graph neural networks. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 25549-25562). PMLR.

[4] Young, A., Wang, F., Wishart, D., Wang, B., Röst, H. and Greiner, R., 2024. FraGNNet: A Deep Probabilistic Model for Mass Spectrum Prediction. arXiv preprint arXiv:2404.02360.

strengths.value: This paper tackles a really important problem and the workflow is realistic, however I have expressed my main concerns about the dataset construction above.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: I would suggest either using stronger simulation methods to construct the simulated data or integrating the experiment data as part of this tool.

title.value: Unraveling Molecular Structure: A Multimodal Spectroscopic Dataset for Chemistry

abstract.value:
Spectroscopic techniques are essential tools for determining the structure of molecules. Different spectroscopic techniques, such as Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), Infrared spectroscopy, and Mass Spectrometry, provide insight into the molecular structure, including the presence or absence of functional groups. Chemists leverage the complementary nature of the different methods to their advantage. However, the lack of a comprehensive multimodal dataset, containing spectra from a variety of spectroscopic techniques, has limited machine-learning approaches mostly to single-modality tasks for predicting molecular structures from spectra. 
Here we introduce a dataset comprising simulated $^1$H-NMR, $^{13}$C-NMR, HSQC-NMR, Infrared, and Mass spectra (positive and negative ion modes) for 790k molecules extracted from chemical reactions in patent data. This dataset enables the development of foundation models for integrating information from multiple spectroscopic modalities, emulating the approach employed by human experts. Additionally, we provide benchmarks for evaluating single-modality tasks such as structure elucidation, predicting the spectra for a target molecule, and functional group predictions. 
This dataset has the potential automate structure elucidation, streamlining the molecular discovery pipeline from synthesis to structure determination. 
The dataset and code for the benchmarks can be found at https://rxn4chemistry.github.io/multimodal-spectroscopic-dataset (Available upon submission of the supporting information).

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
